# Categories in the General Linear Model {#sec-lecture-05}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/setup.R")
library(broom)
library(papaja)
```

```{r}
#| label: data
#| include: false
set.seed(123)

organisation_beta <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data/organisation_beta.csv"))

m_js_high <- mean(organisation_beta$js_score[organisation_beta$salary_c == "high"])
m_js_low <- mean(organisation_beta$js_score[organisation_beta$salary_c == "low"])
lm_c <- lm(js_score ~ salary_c, data = organisation_beta) |> apa_print()
lm_c2 <- lm(js_score ~ salary_c, data = mutate(organisation_beta, salary_c = if_else(salary_c == "low", 1, 2))
) |> apa_print()
lm_c3 <- lm(js_score ~ location, data = organisation_beta) |> aov() |> apa_print()
```

::: {.callout-note .box-goals title="In this chapter"}
After this chapter, you can:

- code a categorical predictor with two categories and say what the intercept and the estimate mean with each coding
- test and report a main effect and an interaction with categorical predictors in jamovi
- read the comparisons with the reference group of a predictor with three or more categories
- test the overall effect of such a predictor with the omnibus ANOVA test
- choose contrast codes that test a precise hypothesis

You need the file `organisation_beta.csv` and jamovi. R is optional.
:::

This chapter explains how categorical predictors are handled in the General Linear Model. It starts with predictors that have only two categories, first for a main effect and then for an interaction effect. It shows how the coding of the categories changes the interpretation of the estimates. Predictors with three or more categories come next: they need an overall test (ANOVA). The chapter ends with contrasts, which make it possible to test more precise hypotheses. The examples use the `organisation_beta.csv` file, with the steps to follow in jamovi and the corresponding outputs from R.

@fig-l05-roadmap shows the path that the chapter follows, from a predictor with two categories to the contrasts.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-roadmap
#| fig-cap: "From a predictor with two categories to the contrasts: the steps of this chapter."
#| fig-alt: "Six boxes in a row joined by arrows. 2 categories: one estimate, the difference. Coding: 0 and 1, or -0.5 and 0.5. Interaction: the product of the codes. 3+ categories: comparisons with a reference. ANOVA: one overall test. Contrasts: codes for one hypothesis."
#| fig-height: 1.4
roadmap <- tribble(
  ~step,            ~detail,
  "2 categories",   "one estimate:\nthe difference",
  "Coding",         "0 and 1, or\n-0.5 and 0.5",
  "Interaction",    "the product\nof the codes",
  "3+ categories",  "comparisons\nwith a reference",
  "ANOVA",          "one overall\ntest",
  "Contrasts",      "codes for one\nhypothesis"
)

flow_chart(roadmap)
```

**Recap.** In @sec-lecture-04, "linear model", "linear regression", "multiple regression" or simply "regression" were all presented as the same model: the **General Linear Model**. It contains one continuous outcome (dependent variable) and one or more categorical or continuous predictors (independent variables), made of main and/or interaction effects:

$$Y = b_{0} + b_{1}\,Predictor\,1 + b_{2}\,Predictor\,2+ ... + b_{n}\,Predictor\,n + e$$

A linear regression is used **to test all the hypotheses at once** and to calculate the predictors' estimates. Specific tests such as the $t$-test or ANOVA are available for certain types of hypotheses, but as they are special cases of linear regressions, their importance is limited (see [Jonas Kristoffer Lindeløv's blog post: Common statistical tests are linear models](https://lindeloev.github.io/tests-as-linear/)).

Once the best line is found, software calculates each estimate. The intercept $b_0$ has no interest for hypothesis testing. Each of $b_1, ..., b_n$ is the slope of the best line between a predictor and the outcome. Each slope is used to test one hypothesis and indicates **how many units the outcome variable increases, decreases or changes when the predictor increases by 1 unit**. If an estimate is 0, the regression line is horizontal, the outcome does not change when the predictor increases and the null hypothesis is not rejected. <!-- check: the recap slide reads "the null alternative hypothesis" -->If an estimate is above or below 0, the regression line is positive or negative and the outcome increases or decreases by $b$. The null hypothesis is then rejected, so the alternative hypothesis is considered plausible. <!-- check: as on the slide, but the next paragraph says that an estimate different from 0 is not enough to reject the null hypothesis (an estimate of 0.35 can be non significant), so the two paragraphs contradict each other -->

The statistical significance of an estimate depends on the **strength of the relationship** and on the **sample size**. An estimate of $b_1 = 0.02$ can be very small but still significantly different from 0. An estimate of $b_1 = 0.35$ can be stronger but in fact not significantly different from 0. The significance is the probability of obtaining your results with your sample in the null hypothesis scenario. It is also called the $p$-value and is between 0% and 100% (a value between 0.0 and 1.0). **If the $p$-value is lower than 5% or 0.05, the probability of obtaining your results in the null hypothesis scenario is low enough to say that the null hypothesis is rejected and that there must be a link between the variables.** <!-- check: as on the slide, but a p-value below 0.05 is evidence of a link, not proof of one, so "there must be a link" is stronger than the test supports -->Remember that the $p$-value is the probability of the data given the null hypothesis: $P(data|H_0)$.

## Hypotheses with categorical predictors having two categories {#sec-l05-two-categories}

This section goes in depth into the processing of categorical predictor variables with linear regressions. Two questions come up:

- How to analyse a predictor with **only two categories**?
- How to analyse a predictor with **more than two categories**?

The first question is addressed in this section and in the next two, the second in the sections that follow.

### Coding a categorical variable

Imagine we sample male and female employees to see whether the difference between their job satisfaction averages is due **to sampling luck or is reflecting a real difference in the population**. That is, **is the difference between male and female employees statistically significant?** @tbl-l05-employees shows the data, which come from the `organisation_beta.csv` file.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-employees
#| tbl-cap: "Gender and job satisfaction score (js_score) of each employee."
organisation_beta |>
  dplyr::select(employee, gender, js_score) |>
  kable()
```

Using a categorical variable having two categories, **for example comparing female and male employees**, is the same as **comparing female employees coded 1 and male employees coded 2** (@fig-l05-gender-codes). In both panels, the black points are the employees and the blue points are the averages of each category.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-gender-codes
#| fig-cap: "Job satisfaction of female and male employees, with the two categories shown as words and as codes."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Female and male as categories."
#|   - "Female coded 1 and male coded 2."
#| fig-alt:
#|   - "Dot plot of job satisfaction for the categories female and male. Black dots are the employees and a blue dot marks the average of each category."
#|   - "The same dot plot with the categories replaced by the codes 1 for female and 2 for male on a numeric axis."
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 3.3
#| fig-height: 3.6
organisation_beta |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gender, y = js_score)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 5) +
  stat_summary(fun = "mean", colour = book_col("blue"), size = 6, geom = "point")

organisation_beta |>
  mutate(gender_c = case_when(
    gender == "female" ~ 1,
    gender == "male" ~ 2
  )) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gender_c, y = js_score)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 5) +
  stat_summary(fun = "mean", colour = book_col("blue"), size = 6, geom = "point") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 2), limits = c(0.5, 2.5))
```

By default, categorical variables **are coded using the alphabetical order** (here female first, then male) with 1, 2, 3 and so on. However, you can recode the variable yourself, with your own order, by creating a new variable with an IF statement (for example `IF(gender == "female", 2, 1)` in jamovi). <!-- check: as on the slide, but jamovi and R do not code the categories 1, 2, 3 by default: they use dummy coding, where the alphabetical order only decides which category is the reference level (coded 0). The jamovi screenshots of this chapter show it: the intercept of 7.75 is marked "reference level" and is the average of the high salary group, whereas the default coding "high = 1, low = 2" would give an intercept of 9.63. The same applies to the two other places where the default coding is described (the next subsection and the report of the main effect) -->

::: {.callout-note .box-definition title="Definition: reference level"}
When a categorical predictor is set as a Factor, jamovi and R use **dummy coding**. The **reference level**, by default the first category in alphabetical order, is coded 0 and the other category is coded 1. The intercept is then the average of the reference level, and the estimate is the difference between the other category and the reference level. For $salary\_c$, the reference level is "high" and the estimate is low minus high: $`r format_number(m_js_low)` - `r format_number(m_js_high)` = `r format_number(m_js_low - m_js_high)`$.
:::

### Default and manual coding in a linear regression

A linear regression of $js\_score$ on the coded gender (a variable called `gender_c`) can be run with either coding. With the **default** coding, female is coded 1 and male is coded 2 (@fig-l05-gender-default and @tbl-l05-gender-default).

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-gender-default
#| fig-cap: "Job satisfaction by gender with female coded 1 and male coded 2 (default coding)."
#| fig-alt: "Dot plot of job satisfaction against the codes 1 for female and 2 for male. Black dots are the employees and a blue dot marks the average at each code."
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "70%"
organisation_beta <- organisation_beta |>
  mutate(gender_c = case_when(
    gender == "female" ~ 1,
    gender == "male" ~ 2
  ))

organisation_beta |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gender_c, y = js_score)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 5) +
  stat_summary(fun = "mean", colour = book_col("blue"), size = 6, geom = "point") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 2), limits = c(0.5, 2.5))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-gender-default
#| tbl-cap: "Linear regression of js_score on gender_c, with female coded 1 and male coded 2."
lm(formula = js_score ~ gender_c, data = organisation_beta) |>
  tidy() |>
  mutate(p.value = format.pval(round(p.value, 3), eps = 0.001)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

With the **manual** coding, male is coded 1 and female is coded 2 (@fig-l05-gender-manual and @tbl-l05-gender-manual).

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-gender-manual
#| fig-cap: "Job satisfaction by gender with male coded 1 and female coded 2 (manual coding)."
#| fig-alt: "Dot plot of job satisfaction against the codes 1 for male and 2 for female. Black dots are the employees and a blue dot marks the average at each code."
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "70%"
organisation_beta <- organisation_beta |>
  mutate(gender_c = case_when(
    gender == "female" ~ 2,
    gender == "male" ~ 1
  ))

organisation_beta |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gender_c, y = js_score)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 5) +
  stat_summary(fun = "mean", colour = book_col("blue"), size = 6, geom = "point") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 2), limits = c(0.5, 2.5))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-gender-manual
#| tbl-cap: "Linear regression of js_score on gender_c, with male coded 1 and female coded 2."
lm(data = organisation_beta, formula = js_score ~ gender_c) |>
  tidy() |>
  mutate(p.value = format.pval(round(p.value, 3), eps = 0.001)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

Between the two tables, the estimate of `gender_c` and its $t$ value change sign whereas the $p$-value stays the same.

### A categorical predictor with two categories {#sec-l05-salary}

Let us use another example with the `organisation_beta.csv` file.

**Variable transformation.** Instead of using $salary$ as a **continuous variable**, let us convert it into $salary\_c$, which is a **categorical variable**:

- everything higher than or equal to the salary average is labelled "**high**" salary
- everything lower than the salary average is labelled "**low**" salary

**Hypothesis.** The $js\_score$ of employees having a **high** $salary\_c$ is different than the $js\_score$ of employees having a **low** $salary\_c$. In mathematical terms:

$$H_a: \mu(js\_score)_{high\,salary} \neq \mu(js\_score)_{low\,salary}$$
$$H_0: \mu(js\_score)_{high\,salary} = \mu(js\_score)_{low\,salary}$$

A hypothesis of differences between two groups is easily tested with a linear regression:

- if $\mu_{1} \neq \mu_{2}$, the slope of the line between these averages is not null (i.e., $b_{1} \neq 0$)
- if $\mu_{1} = \mu_{2}$, the slope of the line between these averages is null (i.e., $b_{1} = 0$)

Comparing the difference between two averages is the same as comparing the slope of the line crossing these two averages. If the two averages are **not equal**, then **the slope of the line crossing them is not 0**. If they are **equal**, then **the slope of the line crossing them is 0**. @fig-l05-slope shows the line crossing the two averages of $js\_score$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-slope
#| fig-cap: "Job satisfaction of employees with a high or low salary: the blue bars are the two averages, the red line crosses them and the dashed line marks the value halfway between them."
#| fig-alt: "Points of job satisfaction for the salary categories high and low, spread slightly sideways. Blue horizontal bars mark the average of each category, a red line joins the two averages and slopes downwards from high to low, and a dashed horizontal line marks the value halfway between the two averages. The plot caption reads: high coded 1 and low coded 2 (default)."
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: "60%"
organisation_beta |>
  ggplot(aes(x = salary_c, y = js_score)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
  geom_segment(x = 1, xend = 2, y = m_js_high, yend = m_js_low, lwd = 2, color = book_col("red")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = (m_js_high + m_js_low)/2, linetype = "dashed") +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "errorbar", aes(ymax = ..y.., ymin = ..y..), lwd = 2, color = book_col("blue")) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  labs(caption = "high coded 1 and low coded 2 (default)")
```

::: {.callout-important title="Warning"}
jamovi and other software **automatically code categorical variables following the alphabetical order** but sometimes you need to change these codes.
:::

For example, here **low coded with the value 1** and **high coded with the value 2** would make more sense (@fig-l05-slope-recoded). The way categorical variables are coded influences the sign of the estimate (positive vs. negative), but **it does not change the value of the statistical test** nor the $p$-value obtained. <!-- check: as on the slide, but the $t$ value changes sign with the coding (-2.88 or 2.88 here): only its size and the $p$-value stay the same -->

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-slope-recoded
#| fig-cap: "The same plot with low coded 1 and high coded 2."
#| fig-alt: "Points of job satisfaction for the salary categories low and high, spread slightly sideways. Blue horizontal bars mark the average of each category, a red line joins the two averages and now slopes upwards from low to high, and a dashed horizontal line marks the value halfway between the two averages."
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: "60%"
organisation_beta |>
  mutate(salary_c = factor(salary_c, levels = c("low", "high"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = salary_c, y = js_score)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
  geom_segment(x = 1, xend = 2, yend = m_js_high, y = m_js_low, lwd = 2, color = book_col("red")) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = (m_js_high + m_js_low)/2, linetype = "dashed") +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "errorbar", aes(ymax = ..y.., ymin = ..y..), lwd = 2, color = book_col("blue")) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
    )
```

**To test the influence of a categorical predictor** variable, either nominal or ordinal, **having two categories** (e.g., high vs. low, male vs. female, France vs. Ireland), it is possible to **test whether the $b$ associated with this predictor is significantly higher, lower, or different from 0**:

$$js\_score = b_{0} + b_{1}\,salary\_c + e$$

::: {.callout-note .box-report title="How to report: a predictor with two categories"}
The template to report the results is exactly the same as for continuous predictors (@sec-lecture-04):

> The predictions provided by the alternative model are significantly better than those provided by the null model (`r lm_c2$full_result$modelfit$r2`).

> The effect of $salary\_c$ on $js\_score$ is statistically significant, therefore $H_0$ can be rejected (`r lm_c2$full_result$salary_c`).
:::

## Testing main effects with categorical predictors {#sec-l05-main}

### Testing a categorical predictor in jamovi

::: {.callout-tip .box-howto title="In jamovi: a linear regression with a categorical predictor"}
To test a categorical predictor in jamovi:

1. Open your file
2. Set the variables in their **correct type**
3. Go to **Analyses > Regression > Linear Regression**
4. Set $js\_score$ as DV (dependent variable) and $salary\_c$ as Factors (i.e., categorical predictor)
:::

@fig-l05-jamovi-main shows the result. The Model Coefficients table has one row for the intercept, marked as the reference level, and one row for $salary\_c$, which compares "low" with "high".

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-jamovi-main
#| fig-cap: "Linear regression of js_score on the categorical predictor salary_c in jamovi."
#| fig-alt: "Screenshot of the jamovi Linear Regression window. The variable js_score is in the Dependent Variable box and salary_c is in the Factors box. The results show the Model Fit Measures, with R of 0.56 and R squared of 0.31, and the Model Coefficients for js_score: an intercept of 7.75 (p below .001, marked as the reference level) and a salary_c row for low minus high with an estimate of minus 1.87, a standard error of 0.65, a t value of minus 2.88 and a p value of 0.010."
#| out-width: "100%"
include_img("jamovi_lm_main_c2.png")
```

::: {.callout-note .box-further collapse="true" title="In R: the same model"}
In R, a variable that contains text is treated as a categorical predictor. `lm()` uses dummy coding with the first category in alphabetical order, "high", as the reference level, so the row `salary_clow` is low minus high, as in jamovi.

```{r}
#| echo: true
lm(js_score ~ salary_c, data = organisation_beta) |>
  summary()
```
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-report title="How to report: the model and the effect of salary_c"}
The model is communicated as follows:

> The prediction provided by the model with all predictors is significantly better than a model without predictors (`r lm_c$full_result$modelfit$r2`).

The hypothesis is communicated as follows, first with the default coding (high = 1 vs. low = 2): <!-- check: see the comment on the default coding above (jamovi and R use dummy coding) -->

> The effect of $salary\_c$ on $js\_score$ is statistically significant, therefore $H_{0}$ can be rejected (`r lm_c$full_result$salary_c`).

and then with the manual coding (low = 1 vs. high = 2):

> The effect of $salary\_c$ on $js\_score$ is statistically significant, therefore $H_{0}$ can be rejected (`r lm_c2$full_result$salary_c`).
:::

### Coding of categorical predictors {#sec-l05-coding-categories}

Choosing 1 and 2 as codes is **just arbitrary**: any other possibility will produce the same $p$-value. However, choosing codes separated by 1 is handy because it is easily interpretable: **the estimate corresponds to the change from one category to another**:

> The $js\_score$ of "high" $salary\_c$ employees is `r round(m_js_high - m_js_low, 2)` higher than the $js\_score$ of "low" $salary\_c$ employees (when "low" is coded 1 and "high" coded 2).

Two special cases are worth knowing: dummy coding and deviation coding.

### Dummy coding {#sec-l05-dummy}

**Dummy coding** is the special case where one category is coded 0 and the other is coded 1. Then the intercept corresponds to the category coded 0 and is the value of $js\_score$ when the predictor is 0. <!-- check: the slide reads "when salary is 0" -->The test of the intercept is the test of the average of the category coded 0 against an average of 0. This is called a **simple effect**. Dummy coding is useful because one of the categories becomes the intercept and is tested against 0.

For example, in jamovi, recode female as 0 and male as 1 with `IF(gender == "female", 0, 1)`. @fig-l05-gender-dummy and @tbl-l05-gender-dummy show the result.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-gender-dummy
#| fig-cap: "Job satisfaction by gender with female coded 0 and male coded 1 (dummy coding)."
#| fig-alt: "Dot plot of job satisfaction against the codes 0 for female and 1 for male. Black dots are the employees and a blue dot marks the average at each code."
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "70%"
organisation_beta <- organisation_beta |>
  mutate(gender_c = case_when(
    gender == "female" ~ 0,
    gender == "male" ~ 1
  ))

organisation_beta |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gender_c, y = js_score)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 5) +
  stat_summary(fun = "mean", colour = book_col("blue"), size = 6, geom = "point") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1), limits = c(-0.5, 1.5))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-gender-dummy
#| tbl-cap: "Linear regression of js_score on gender_c, with female coded 0 and male coded 1."
lm(data = organisation_beta, formula = js_score ~ gender_c) |>
  broom::tidy() |>
  dplyr::mutate(p.value = format.pval(round(p.value, 3), eps = 0.001)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

### Deviation coding {#sec-l05-deviation}

**Deviation coding** is the special case where the intercept is situated between the codes of the categories, for example when one category is coded 1 and the other -1. Then the intercept corresponds to the average between the two categories and the test of the intercept is the test of the average for the variable. <!-- check: with groups of different sizes this intercept is the average of the two group averages (6.85 here, with 8 women and 12 men), not the average of all the employees (6.81) --> Deviation coding is useful because **the average of the categories becomes the intercept** and is tested against 0.

For example, in jamovi, recode female as -1 and male as 1 with `IF(gender == "female", -1, 1)`.

However, with a deviation coding using -1 vs. +1, **the distance between the categories is 2**, not 1. Therefore, even if the test of the slope is exactly the same, the value of the slope (the estimate) is half as large and so not as easy to interpret. Consequently, it is possible to use **a deviation coding with -0.5 vs. +0.5 to keep the distance of 1** between the categories. For example, in jamovi, recode female as -0.5 and male as 0.5 with `IF(gender == "female", -0.5, 0.5)`.

@fig-l05-gender-deviation-1 and @tbl-l05-gender-deviation-1 show the result with female = -1 and male = 1.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-gender-deviation-1
#| fig-cap: "Job satisfaction by gender with female coded -1 and male coded 1 (deviation coding)."
#| fig-alt: "Dot plot of job satisfaction against the codes -1 for female and 1 for male. Black dots are the employees and a blue dot marks the average at each code."
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "70%"
organisation_beta <- organisation_beta |>
  mutate(gender_c = case_when(
    gender == "female" ~ -1,
    gender == "male" ~ 1
  ))

organisation_beta |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gender_c, y = js_score)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 5) +
  stat_summary(fun = "mean", colour = book_col("blue"), size = 6, geom = "point") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-1, 1), limits = c(-1.5, 1.5))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-gender-deviation-1
#| tbl-cap: "Linear regression of js_score on gender_c, with female coded -1 and male coded 1."
lm(data = organisation_beta, formula = js_score ~ gender_c) |>
  broom::tidy() |>
  dplyr::mutate(p.value = format.pval(round(p.value, 3), eps = 0.001)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

@fig-l05-gender-deviation-05 and @tbl-l05-gender-deviation-05 show the result with female = -0.5 and male = 0.5.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-gender-deviation-05
#| fig-cap: "Job satisfaction by gender with female coded -0.5 and male coded 0.5 (deviation coding)."
#| fig-alt: "Dot plot of job satisfaction against the codes -0.5 for female and 0.5 for male. Black dots are the employees and a blue dot marks the average at each code."
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "70%"
organisation_beta <- organisation_beta |>
  mutate(gender_c = case_when(
    gender == "female" ~ -0.5,
    gender == "male" ~ 0.5
  ))

organisation_beta |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gender_c, y = js_score)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 5) +
  stat_summary(fun = "mean", colour = book_col("blue"), size = 6, geom = "point") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-0.5, 0.5), limits = c(-1, 1))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-gender-deviation-05
#| tbl-cap: "Linear regression of js_score on gender_c, with female coded -0.5 and male coded 0.5."
lm(data = organisation_beta, formula = js_score ~ gender_c) |>
  broom::tidy() |>
  dplyr::mutate(p.value = format.pval(round(p.value, 3), eps = 0.001)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: gender-codings
#| include: false
gender_codings <- organisation_beta |>
  mutate(
    code_dummy = if_else(gender == "female", 0, 1),
    code_deviation_1 = if_else(gender == "female", -1, 1),
    code_deviation_05 = if_else(gender == "female", -0.5, 0.5)
  )

model_gender_dummy <- lm(js_score ~ code_dummy, data = gender_codings)
model_gender_deviation_1 <- lm(js_score ~ code_deviation_1, data = gender_codings)
model_gender_deviation_05 <- lm(js_score ~ code_deviation_05, data = gender_codings)

gender_means <- organisation_beta |>
  group_by(gender) |>
  summarise(js_score = mean(js_score))

mean_female <- gender_means$js_score[gender_means$gender == "female"]
mean_male <- gender_means$js_score[gender_means$gender == "male"]
p_gender <- broom::tidy(model_gender_dummy)$p.value[2]
```

@fig-l05-three-codings puts the three codings side by side. The two averages do not move: only the codes on the horizontal axis change. The intercept is the value of the line at the code 0, and the estimate is its slope.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-three-codings
#| fig-cap: "The same two averages of job satisfaction (blue points) with three codings of gender. The blue line joins the averages: its value at the code 0 (orange) is the intercept $b_0$, and its slope is the estimate $b_1$."
#| fig-alt: "Three panels of job satisfaction against the code of gender, with the 20 employees as grey points and the average of each gender as a blue point joined by a blue line. Left, dummy coding with female 0 and male 1: the orange intercept sits on the female average, b0 = 7.02 and b1 = -0.34. Middle, deviation coding with female -1 and male 1: the orange intercept sits halfway between the averages, b0 = 6.85 and b1 = -0.17. Right, deviation coding with female -0.5 and male 0.5: b0 = 6.85 and b1 = -0.34."
#| fig-height: 3.6
codings <- tribble(
  ~coding,                            ~code_female, ~code_male, ~label_x, ~label_hjust, ~label_shift,
  "Dummy coding: 0 and 1",            0,            1,          -0.1,    1,            0,
  "Deviation: -1 and 1",     -1,           1,          0,        0.5,          -0.6,
  "Deviation: -0.5 and 0.5", -0.5,         0.5,        0,        0.5,          -0.6
) |>
  mutate(
    intercept = c(coef(model_gender_dummy)[[1]], coef(model_gender_deviation_1)[[1]], coef(model_gender_deviation_05)[[1]]),
    slope = c(coef(model_gender_dummy)[[2]], coef(model_gender_deviation_1)[[2]], coef(model_gender_deviation_05)[[2]]),
    estimates = paste0("list(b[0] == '", format_number(intercept), "', b[1] == '", format_number(slope), "')"),
    coding = factor(coding, levels = coding)
  )

coded_employees <- codings |>
  tidyr::crossing(organisation_beta |> select(employee, gender, js_score)) |>
  mutate(code = if_else(gender == "female", code_female, code_male))

coded_means <- codings |>
  tidyr::crossing(gender_means) |>
  mutate(code = if_else(gender == "female", code_female, code_male))

axis_room <- tribble(
  ~coding,                            ~code,
  "Dummy coding: 0 and 1",          -0.75,
  "Dummy coding: 0 and 1",          1.35,
  "Deviation: -1 and 1",     -1.6,
  "Deviation: -1 and 1",     1.6,
  "Deviation: -0.5 and 0.5", -0.8,
  "Deviation: -0.5 and 0.5", 0.8
) |>
  mutate(coding = factor(coding, levels = levels(codings$coding)))

# The ticks of each panel are the codes of that panel and 0.
codes_on_axis <- function(limits) {
  if (limits[2] > 1.5) return(c(-1, 0, 1))
  if (limits[2] > 1.1) return(c(0, 1))
  c(-0.5, 0, 0.5)
}

ggplot(coded_employees, aes(code, js_score)) +
  geom_blank(data = axis_room, aes(x = code, y = 5)) +
  geom_point(colour = book_col("grey"), size = 2) +
  geom_segment(
    data = codings,
    aes(x = code_female, xend = code_male, y = intercept + slope * code_female, yend = intercept + slope * code_male),
    colour = book_col("blue"), linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(data = coded_means, colour = book_col("blue"), size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = codings, aes(x = 0, y = intercept), colour = book_col("orange"), size = 3.2) +
  geom_text(data = codings, aes(x = label_x, y = intercept + label_shift, hjust = label_hjust, label = "intercept"), size = 3.4) +
  geom_text(data = codings, aes(x = (code_female + code_male) / 2, y = 10.9, label = estimates), parse = TRUE, size = 3.6) +
  geom_text(data = coded_means, aes(x = code, y = 2.6, label = gender), size = 3.4) +
  facet_wrap(~coding, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = codes_on_axis) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(2.3, 11.2), breaks = seq(4, 10, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Code of gender", y = "js_score")
```

::: {.callout-tip .box-example title="Example: the same two averages with three codings"}
Women have an average $js\_score$ of `r format_number(mean_female)` and men of `r format_number(mean_male)`.

- Dummy coding (0 and 1): $b_0 = `r format_number(coef(model_gender_dummy)[[1]])`$, the average of women, and $b_1 = `r format_number(coef(model_gender_dummy)[[2]])`$, men minus women.
- Deviation coding (-1 and 1): $b_0 = `r format_number(coef(model_gender_deviation_1)[[1]])`$ and $b_1 = `r format_number(coef(model_gender_deviation_1)[[2]])`$, half of the difference.
- Deviation coding (-0.5 and 0.5): $b_0 = `r format_number(coef(model_gender_deviation_05)[[1]])`$ and $b_1 = `r format_number(coef(model_gender_deviation_05)[[2]])`$, the difference.

The $p$-value of $b_1$ is `r sub("p = ", "", format_p(p_gender))` with all three codings. With deviation coding, $b_0$ is the average of the two group averages; it is not the average of the 20 employees (`r format_number(mean(organisation_beta$js_score))`), because there are `r sum(organisation_beta$gender == "female")` women and `r sum(organisation_beta$gender == "male")` men.
:::

## Testing interaction effects with categorical predictors {#sec-l05-interaction}

::: {.callout-tip .box-howto title="In jamovi: an interaction between two categorical predictors"}
To test an interaction between categorical predictors in jamovi:

1. Open your file
2. Set the variables according to their type
3. Go to **Analyses > Regression > Linear Regression**
4. Set $js\_score$ as DV and both $salary\_c$ and $gender$ as Factors
5. In the **Model Builder** option, select both $salary\_c$ and $gender$ to bring them in the Factors at once <!-- check: the screenshot shows the two predictors moved to Block 1 of the Model Builder, not to Factors -->
:::

The model tested is:

$$js\_score = b_{0} + b_{1}\,salary\_c + b_{2}\,gender + b_{3}\,salary\_c*gender + e$$

Note that the test of the interaction effect corresponds to the test of a variable resulting from the multiplication between the codes of $salary\_c$ and the codes of $gender$. @fig-l05-jamovi-interaction shows the result in jamovi. In the Model Builder, Block 1 contains $salary\_c$, $gender$ and their interaction. The Model Coefficients table has one row for the intercept, one row for each of $salary\_c$ and $gender$, and one row for the interaction.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-jamovi-interaction
#| fig-cap: "Linear regression of js_score on salary_c, gender and their interaction in jamovi."
#| fig-alt: "Screenshot of the jamovi Linear Regression window. The variable js_score is the dependent variable and salary_c and gender are in the Factors box. In the Model Builder, Block 1 contains salary_c, gender and salary_c times gender. The results show Model Fit Measures with R of 0.57 and R squared of 0.32, and Model Coefficients with an intercept of 7.93 and rows for salary_c (low minus high, estimate minus 1.82, p of 0.113), gender (male minus female, estimate minus 0.29, p of 0.771) and the interaction (estimate minus 0.09, p of 0.947)."
#| out-width: "100%"
include_img("jamovi_lm_main_cint.png")
```

```{r}
#| label: interaction-means
#| include: false
model_salary_c_gender <- lm(js_score ~ salary_c * gender, data = organisation_beta)

cell_means <- organisation_beta |>
  group_by(salary_c, gender) |>
  summarise(js_score = mean(js_score), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(salary_c = factor(salary_c, levels = c("high", "low")))

cell_mean <- function(salary_level, gender_level) {
  cell_means$js_score[cell_means$salary_c == salary_level & cell_means$gender == gender_level]
}

difference_female <- cell_mean("low", "female") - cell_mean("high", "female")
difference_male <- cell_mean("low", "male") - cell_mean("high", "male")
```

@fig-l05-interaction-means draws the four averages of the model, one line per gender. Without an interaction, the two lines would be parallel: the difference between a low and a high salary would be the same for women and for men. Here the lines are almost parallel, which agrees with the estimate of the interaction, close to 0 and not significant.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-interaction-means
#| fig-cap: "The average job satisfaction of the four groups of the interaction model, one line per gender. The lines are almost parallel: the effect of salary_c is about the same for women and for men."
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of the average js_score for a high and a low salary_c. A blue line for female goes from 7.93 to 6.11 and a red line for male goes from 7.63 to 5.72. The two lines fall by almost the same amount and are almost parallel."
#| fig-height: 3.4
cell_means |>
  mutate(label_position = if_else(gender == "female", js_score + 0.3, js_score - 0.3)) |>
  ggplot(aes(salary_c, js_score, colour = gender, group = gender)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(y = label_position, label = format_number(js_score)), colour = book_col("ink"), size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(female = book_col("blue"), male = book_col("red"))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(5, 8.5)) +
  labs(x = "salary_c", y = "Average js_score")
```

::: {.callout-tip .box-example title="Example: the interaction as a difference of differences"}
The reference levels are "high" for $salary\_c$ and "female" for $gender$. For women, low minus high is `r format_number(difference_female)`: this is the estimate of $salary\_c$. For men, low minus high is `r format_number(difference_male)`. The estimate of the interaction is the difference between the two: $`r format_number(difference_male)` - (`r format_number(difference_female)`) = `r format_number(coef(model_salary_c_gender)[["salary_clow:gendermale"]])`$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-further collapse="true" title="In R: the same model"}
The formula `salary_c * gender` asks for the two main effects and their interaction. The reference levels are "high" and "female", so the rows are called `salary_clow`, `gendermale` and `salary_clow:gendermale`.

```{r}
#| echo: true
lm(js_score ~ salary_c * gender, data = organisation_beta) |>
  summary()
```
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-demo title="Live demonstration"}
In the lecture, a model with an interaction between categorical predictors is run live in jamovi before the exercise below.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .box-yourturn title="Your turn: test two interaction models"}
With the `organisation_beta.csv` data, test the following models and conclude on each effect:

Model 1: $js\_score = b_{0} + b_{1}\,perf + b_{2}\,gender + b_{3}\,perf*gender + e$

Model 2: $js\_score = b_{0} + b_{1}\,perf + b_{2}\,location + b_{3}\,perf*location+ e$

Suggested time: 10 minutes.
:::

## Hypotheses with a categorical predictor having three or more categories {#sec-l05-three-categories}

### Predictors with three or more categories {#sec-l05-three-coding}

I would like to test the effect of the variable $location$, which has three categories: "Ireland", "France" and "Australia". @fig-l05-jamovi-three shows the result in jamovi.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-jamovi-three
#| fig-cap: "Linear regression of js_score on the three-category predictor location in jamovi."
#| fig-alt: "Screenshot of the jamovi Linear Regression window. The variable js_score is the dependent variable and location is in the Factors box. The results show Model Fit Measures with R of 0.53 and R squared of 0.28, and Model Coefficients with an intercept of 6.21 and two rows for location: France minus Australia, with an estimate of 0.06 and a p value of 0.948, and Ireland minus Australia, with an estimate of 1.95 and a p value of 0.031."
#| out-width: "100%"
include_img("jamovi_lm_main_c31.png")
```

In the Model Coefficients table, to test the estimate of $location$, there is not one result for $location$ but two! They are:

- the comparison of "Australia" vs. "France"
- the comparison of "Australia" vs. "Ireland"

**Why are multiple $p$-values provided for the same predictor?**

To understand why, take the following variables:

- Outcome = $js\_score$ (from 0 to 10)
- Predictor = $location$ (three categories: *Australia*, *France* and *Ireland*)

@tbl-l05-location-data and @fig-l05-location show the data.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-location-data
#| tbl-cap: "Location and job satisfaction score (js_score) of each employee."
organisation_beta |>
  select(employee, location, js_score) |>
  kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-location
#| fig-cap: "Job satisfaction of the employees working in Australia, France and Ireland."
#| fig-alt: "Dot plot of job satisfaction for the locations Australia, France and Ireland. Black dots are the employees and a blue dot marks the average of each location."
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "70%"
organisation_beta |>
  ggplot(aes(location, js_score)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 5) +
  stat_summary(fun = "mean", colour = book_col("blue"), size = 6, geom = "point") +
  scale_x_discrete("location")
```

A $t$-test can only compare two categories. Because linear regression models are (kind of) $t$-tests, the categories are compared two by two, with one category as the reference to compare all the others. For example, a linear regression of $location$ on $js\_score$ <!-- check: as on the slide, but the model has js_score as the outcome and location as the predictor (js_score ~ location), so "of js_score on location" would be exact --> displays not one effect for $location$ but the effects of the two-by-two comparisons, using a reference group chosen by alphabetical order (@tbl-l05-location-lm). In this table, `locationFrance` is the comparison of France with the reference group and `locationIreland` the comparison of Ireland with the reference group.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-location-lm
#| tbl-cap: "Linear regression of js_score on location, with Australia as the reference group."
lm(data = organisation_beta, formula = js_score ~ location) |>
  tidy() |>
  mutate(p.value = format.pval(round(p.value, 3), eps = 0.001)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

In our case the reference is the group "Australia" (first letter).

```{r}
#| label: location-models
#| include: false
model_location <- lm(js_score ~ location, data = organisation_beta)

organisation_beta_france <- organisation_beta |>
  mutate(location = relevel(factor(location), ref = "France"))
model_location_france <- lm(js_score ~ location, data = organisation_beta_france)

location_means <- organisation_beta |>
  group_by(location) |>
  summarise(js_score = mean(js_score))

location_mean <- function(place) {
  location_means$js_score[location_means$location == place]
}

location_estimates <- broom::tidy(model_location)
location_p <- function(term_name) {
  location_estimates$p.value[location_estimates$term == term_name]
}
```

@fig-l05-reference shows what the two rows of the table measure. The intercept is the average of Australia, and each estimate is the distance between the average of one location and the average of Australia.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-reference
#| fig-cap: "Job satisfaction by location. The intercept is the average of the reference group, Australia (dashed line), and each estimate is the distance from this line to the average of another location (blue segments)."
#| fig-alt: "Dot plot of job satisfaction for Australia, France and Ireland, with the employees as grey points and the average of each location as a blue point. A blue dashed line at 6.21 marks the average of Australia, labelled reference group, intercept = 6.21. A short blue segment next to France is labelled France minus Australia, b = 0.06. A long blue segment next to Ireland, from 6.21 to 8.16, is labelled Ireland minus Australia, b = 1.95."
#| fig-height: 3.8
reference_mean <- location_mean("Australia")

location_comparisons <- location_means |>
  mutate(position = as.numeric(factor(location))) |>
  filter(location != "Australia") |>
  mutate(
    estimate = js_score - reference_mean,
    label = paste0(location, " - Australia\nb = ", format_number(estimate))
  )

ggplot(organisation_beta, aes(location, js_score)) +
  geom_point(colour = book_col("grey"), size = 2.2, position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 1005)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = reference_mean, colour = book_col("blue"), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_segment(
    data = location_comparisons,
    aes(x = position + 0.22, xend = position + 0.22, y = reference_mean, yend = js_score),
    colour = book_col("blue"), linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  geom_point(data = location_means, colour = book_col("blue"), size = 3.5) +
  geom_text(
    data = location_comparisons,
    aes(x = position + 0.3, y = if_else(estimate > 0.5, (reference_mean + js_score) / 2, js_score + 0.75), label = label),
    hjust = 0, size = 3.4, lineheight = 0.95
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 1.25, y = reference_mean - 0.75, hjust = 0, size = 3.4, lineheight = 0.95,
    label = paste0("reference group\nintercept = ", format_number(reference_mean))
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.5, 0.95))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(3, 10.5), breaks = seq(4, 10, 2)) +
  labs(x = "location", y = "js_score")
```

::: {.callout-tip .box-example title="Example: the two dummy variables of location"}
For a predictor with three categories, the software creates two dummy variables, one per category other than the reference group:

```{r}
#| label: location-dummy-codes
tribble(
  ~location,   ~locationFrance, ~locationIreland,
  "Australia", 0,               0,
  "France",    1,               0,
  "Ireland",   0,               1
) |>
  kable(align = "lcc")
```

The intercept is the average of Australia (`r format_number(coef(model_location)[[1]])`). Adding each estimate gives the other averages: France $`r format_number(coef(model_location)[[1]])` + `r format_number(coef(model_location)[["locationFrance"]])` = `r format_number(location_mean("France"))`$ and Ireland $`r format_number(coef(model_location)[[1]])` + `r format_number(coef(model_location)[["locationIreland"]])` = `r format_number(location_mean("Ireland"))`$.
:::

Here is our problem: **how to test the overall effect of a variable with three or more categories?**

### ANOVA for overall effects {#sec-l05-anova}

Besides linear regression and the $t$-test, researchers use ANOVA a lot. ANOVA stands for Analysis of Variance and is also a subcategory of linear regression models. ANOVA is used to calculate the overall effect of a categorical variable having more than two categories, as the $t$-test cannot cope. In the case of testing one categorical variable, a "one-way" ANOVA is performed.

**How does ANOVA work?** In real words:

- $H_a$: at least one group is different from the others
- $H_0$: all the groups are the same

In mathematical terms:

- $H_a$: it is **not true** that $\mu_{1} = \mu_{2} = \mu_{3}$
- $H_0$: it is **true** that $\mu_{1} = \mu_{2} = \mu_{3}$

I will not go too much into the details but, to check whether at least one group is different from the others, the distance of each value to the overall mean (between-group variation) is compared to the distance of each value to their group mean (within-group variation). <!-- check: the slide defines between-group variation as the distance of each value to the overall mean, whereas the figure defines it as the differences among group means; the distance of each value to the overall mean is the total variation (here the sums of squares are 15.60 between groups, 40.24 within groups and 55.84 in total) -->**If the between-group variation is the same as the within-group variation, all the groups are the same.** <!-- check: as on the slide, but an $F$ value close to 1 only gives no evidence of a difference between the groups; it does not show that the groups are the same --> @fig-l05-anova-basics illustrates both: in panel A, the between-group variation is the difference among the group means, and in panel B, the within-group variation is the variability within each group.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-anova-basics
#| fig-cap: "The two sources of variation compared by a one-way ANOVA: between-group variation (A) and within-group variation (B)."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels showing three bell-shaped distributions in blue, yellow and grey, centred on the values 5, 8 and 11 of a variable called Value. In panel A, titled between-group variation (the differences among group means), double-headed arrows link the three group means. In panel B, titled within-group variation (the variability within each group), a double-headed arrow spans the width of each distribution."
#| out-width: "80%"
include_img("one_way_anova_basics.png")
```

```{r}
#| label: location-anova
#| include: false
location_anova <- anova(model_location)
ss_between <- location_anova["location", "Sum Sq"]
ss_within <- location_anova["Residuals", "Sum Sq"]
df_between <- location_anova["location", "Df"]
df_within <- location_anova["Residuals", "Df"]
f_location <- location_anova["location", "F value"]
p_location <- location_anova["location", "Pr(>F)"]
```

@fig-l05-anova-ss gives the numbers of our example. The total variation of $js\_score$ (a sum of squares of `r format_number(ss_between + ss_within)`) splits in two parts. The variation between groups comes from the distances between each group average and the overall average. The variation within groups comes from the distances between each value and its group average.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-anova-ss
#| fig-cap: "The total variation of job satisfaction in our example (sum of squares) split into the variation between the three locations and the variation within the locations."
#| fig-alt: "One horizontal bar for the total sum of squares of js_score, 55.84. A blue segment of 15.60, or 28%, is the variation between groups. A grey segment of 40.24, or 72%, is the variation within groups."
#| fig-height: 1.9
variation_parts <- tibble(
  part = c("between groups (location)", "within groups (error)"),
  sum_of_squares = c(ss_between, ss_within),
  label_position = c(ss_between / 2, ss_between + ss_within / 2)
) |>
  mutate(
    part = factor(part, levels = rev(part)),
    label = paste0(format_number(sum_of_squares), " (", scales::percent(sum_of_squares / sum(sum_of_squares), accuracy = 1), ")")
  )

ggplot(variation_parts, aes(x = sum_of_squares, y = "variation", fill = part)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5, colour = "white", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(x = label_position, label = label), colour = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 4.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("between groups (location)" = book_col("blue"), "within groups (error)" = book_col("grey")),
    breaks = c("between groups (location)", "within groups (error)")
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = "Sum of squares of js_score", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

::: {.callout-tip .box-example title="Example: the F value of location"}
Each sum of squares is divided by its degrees of freedom to give a mean square, and $F$ is the ratio of the two mean squares: $F = (`r format_number(ss_between)` / `r df_between`) / (`r format_number(ss_within)` / `r df_within`) = `r format_number(ss_between / df_between)` / `r format_number(ss_within / df_within)` = `r format_number(f_location)`$. The mean square between groups is `r format_number(f_location, 1)` times the mean square within groups, but with so few employees this gives $`r format_p(p_location)`$.
:::

### ANOVA in our example {#sec-l05-anova-example}

A hypothesis for a categorical predictor with three or more categories predicts that **at least one group among the three groups will have an average significantly different from the other averages**. The hypothesis is formulated as follows:

> The $js\_score$ of employees working in at least one specific $location$ will be significantly different than the $js\_score$ of employees working in the other $location$.

In mathematical terms:

- $H_0$: it is true that

  $$\mu(js\_score)_{Ireland} = \mu(js\_score)_{France} = \mu(js\_score)_{Australia}$$

- $H_a$: it is **not** true that

  $$\mu(js\_score)_{Ireland} = \mu(js\_score)_{France} = \mu(js\_score)_{Australia}$$

This analysis is usually performed using a one-way ANOVA but, as ANOVA is a special case of the General Linear Model, let us keep this approach. @fig-l05-anova-data shows the three group averages and the overall average.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-anova-data
#| fig-cap: "Job satisfaction by location: the blue bars are the group averages and the dashed line is the overall average."
#| fig-alt: "Points of job satisfaction for Australia, France and Ireland, spread slightly sideways. A blue horizontal bar marks the average of each location and a dashed horizontal line marks the average of all the employees."
#| fig-width: 4.5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| out-width: "70%"
organisation_beta |>
  ggplot(aes(x = location, y =  js_score)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(organisation_beta$js_score), linetype = "dashed") +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "errorbar", aes(ymax = ..y.., ymin = ..y..), lwd = 2, color = book_col("blue")) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

::: {.callout-tip .box-howto title="In jamovi: the omnibus ANOVA test of a categorical predictor"}
To run it in jamovi:

1. Open your file
2. Set the variables according to their type
3. Go to Analyses > Regression > Linear Regression
4. Set $js\_score$ as DV and $location$ as Factors
5. In the **Model Coefficients** option, select **Omnibus ANOVA Test**
:::

@fig-l05-jamovi-anova shows the result. The Omnibus ANOVA Test table gives a single test for $location$, whereas the Model Coefficients table still lists the two comparisons with Australia.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-jamovi-anova
#| fig-cap: "Linear regression of js_score on location with the Omnibus ANOVA test in jamovi."
#| fig-alt: "Screenshot of the jamovi Linear Regression window with js_score as the dependent variable and location in the Factors box. The results show Model Fit Measures with R of 0.53 and R squared of 0.28, an Omnibus ANOVA Test table with a location row (sum of squares 15.60, 2 degrees of freedom, mean square 7.80, F of 3.30, p of 0.062) and a Residuals row (sum of squares 40.24, 17 degrees of freedom, mean square 2.37), and the Model Coefficients table with France minus Australia and Ireland minus Australia."
#| out-width: "100%"
include_img("jamovi_lm_main_c32.png")
```

::: {.callout-note .box-definition title="Definition: omnibus test"}
The **omnibus test** of a categorical predictor is one test of its overall effect. Its null hypothesis is that all the group averages are equal. In jamovi, it is the $F$ test of the row of the predictor in the Omnibus ANOVA Test table.
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-further collapse="true" title="In R: the same model"}
`summary()` gives the comparisons with the reference group, and `anova()` gives the omnibus test, with the sums of squares, the degrees of freedom, the mean squares, $F$ and $p$ of the jamovi table.

```{r}
#| echo: true
lm(js_score ~ location, data = organisation_beta) |>
  anova()
```
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-report title="How to report: the overall effect of a categorical predictor"}
The result is communicated as follows:

> There is no significant effect of employees' $location$ on their average $js\_score$ (`r lm_c3$statistic$location`).
:::

::: {.callout-warning .box-mistake title="Common mistake: concluding on the predictor from one comparison"}
The row Ireland - Australia of the Model Coefficients table is significant ($`r format_p(location_p("locationIreland"))`$), but this does not show an effect of $location$. Each row compares one location with the reference group only. The overall effect is tested by the omnibus test, which is not significant here ($`r format_p(p_location)`$).
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-demo title="Live demonstration"}
In the lecture, the analysis of a predictor with three categories is run live in jamovi before the exercise below.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .box-yourturn title="Your turn: test models with salary, location and performance"}
Using the `organisation_beta.csv` file, test the following models and conclude on the hypothesis related to each estimate:

Model 1: $js\_score = b_{0} + b_{1}\,salary + b_{2}\,location + b_{3}\,perf + e$

Model 2:

$$js\_score = b_{0} + b_{1}\,salary + b_{2}\,location + b_{3}\,perf + b_{4}\,salary*location +$$
$$b_{5}\,perf*location + b_{6}\,perf*salary + b_{7}\,salary*location*perf + e$$

Suggested time: 5 minutes.
:::

## Manipulating contrasts with categorical predictors {#sec-l05-contrasts}

### Post-hoc tests {#sec-l05-posthoc}

Imagine you want to test the specific difference between France and Ireland: **how to obtain a test of specific categories when using a categorical variable with three or more categories?**

The "post-hoc" test runs a separate $t$-test for every pairwise comparison of categories (@tbl-l05-posthoc). <!-- check: as on the slide, but the $p$-values of the table are Tukey-adjusted (ptukey: 1.00, 0.08 and 0.11), which jamovi does by default, whereas separate unadjusted $t$-tests would give 0.948, 0.031 and 0.048 -->

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-posthoc
#| tbl-cap: "Post-hoc tests of the pairwise differences between locations (md: mean difference, ptukey: p-value with the Tukey correction)."
res <- jmv::ANOVA(
    formula = js_score ~ location,
    data = organisation_beta,
    postHoc = ~ location)

res$postHoc[[1]] |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: posthoc-values
#| include: false
posthoc_table <- as.data.frame(res$postHoc[[1]])
tukey_p <- function(first, second) {
  posthoc_table$ptukey[posthoc_table$location1 == first & posthoc_table$location2 == second]
}
p_ireland_france <- broom::tidy(model_location_france) |>
  filter(term == "locationIreland") |>
  pull(p.value)
```

::: {.callout-note .box-definition title="Definition: post-hoc test"}
A **post-hoc test** compares every pair of categories, without a hypothesis for any pair. By default, jamovi corrects the $p$-values for the number of comparisons with the Tukey correction (column `ptukey`), so they are larger than the $p$-values of separate comparisons.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .box-example title="Example: the same comparison with and without the correction"}
Ireland and Australia are compared in the Model Coefficients table ($`r format_p(location_p("locationIreland"))`$) and in the post-hoc table ($p_{tukey} `r sub("p ", "", format_p(tukey_p("Australia", "Ireland")))`$). The same holds for Ireland and France: $`r format_p(p_ireland_france)`$ with France as the reference group, and $p_{tukey} `r sub("p ", "", format_p(tukey_p("France", "Ireland")))`$ here.
:::

Even if it looks useful, a "post-hoc" test can be considered as $p$-hacking because **there is no specific hypothesis testing, everything is compared**. Corrections for multiple tests are available (i.e., Tukey, Scheffe, Bonferroni or Holm) but they are not good practice. <!-- check: as on the slide, but the post-hoc table above already applies a Tukey correction, and a correction for multiple tests is what makes pairwise comparisons acceptable; the problem raised here is the absence of a specific hypothesis -->

### Contrasts or factorial ANOVA {#sec-l05-contrast-rules}

By using specific codes for the categories (also called **contrasts**), it is possible to test more precise hypotheses. Actually, you are mastering contrasts already: when a recoding is done on a variable with two categories (like dummy coding or deviation coding), a contrast is applied.

::: {.callout-note .box-definition title="Definition: contrast"}
A **contrast** is a variable of codes given to the categories of a predictor, so that its estimate tests one chosen comparison between group averages. A predictor with $k$ categories takes at most $k - 1$ contrasts in the same model.
:::

When a recoding is used on more than two categories, three rules have to be applied:

1. **Categories with the same code are tested together.** For example, coding Ireland 1, France 1 and Australia 2 compares Ireland and France versus Australia.
2. **The number of contrasts possible is the number of categories minus 1.** For example, $location$ has three categories so two contrast comparisons can be performed.
3. **The value 0 means the category is not taken into account.** For example, coding Ireland 1, France 0 and Australia 2 compares Ireland versus Australia. <!-- check: as on the slide, but with a single contrast variable coded Ireland 1, France 0 and Australia 2, France is not ignored (in the data the slope is -0.11, p = 0.817); a 0 does mean "not taken into account" when the model holds a complete set of orthogonal contrasts, for example Ireland 1, France 0, Australia -1 together with Ireland 1, France -2, Australia 1 (each contrast sums to zero and so do the products of their codes). With the sum to zero codes of the worked example below, which are not orthogonal, the category coded 0 still counts. With groups of different sizes, as here, a contrast used alone does not leave out its category coded 0 either (1, 0, -1 alone gives 0.94, whereas half of Ireland minus Australia is 0.98) -->

```{r}
#| label: single-contrast
#| include: false
single_contrast <- organisation_beta |>
  mutate(code = case_when(
    location == "Ireland" ~ 1,
    location == "France" ~ 0,
    location == "Australia" ~ 2
  ))

single_contrast_slope <- broom::tidy(lm(js_score ~ code, data = single_contrast)) |>
  filter(term == "code")
```

::: {.callout-warning .box-mistake title="Common mistake: reading every 0 as a category left out"}
A 0 does not always leave a category out. Used alone, the codes Ireland 1, France 0 and Australia 2 place the locations on a line, and France counts in its slope ($b = `r format_number(single_contrast_slope$estimate)`$, $`r format_p(single_contrast_slope$p.value)`$). A category coded 0 is left out when the model holds all the contrasts of the predictor (the number of categories minus 1) and these contrasts are orthogonal: across the categories, the codes of each one sum to 0 and the products of the codes of two contrasts also sum to 0. The polynomial contrasts below are orthogonal.
:::

### Sum to zero contrasts {#sec-l05-sum-zero}

Also called "simple" contrasts, each contrast encodes the difference between one of the groups and a baseline category, which in this case corresponds to the first group. <!-- check: with these codes, the regression coefficients compare each category with the average of the group means rather than with a baseline category (see the worked example below) -->@tbl-l05-sum-zero-example gives the codes of the three categories of a predictor (placebo and two vaccines) and @fig-l05-sum-zero-outcome the outcome of each category.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-sum-zero-example
#| tbl-cap: "Sum to zero contrasts for a predictor with three categories."
contrast_df <-
  tribble(
    ~`Predictor's categories`, ~Contrast1, ~Contrast2,
    "Placebo",                 -1,         -1,
    "Vaccine 1",                1,          0,
    "Vaccine 2",                0,          1
  )

contrast_df |>
  kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-sum-zero-outcome
#| fig-cap: "Outcome of each category of the predictor."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of an outcome for the categories Placebo, Vaccine 1 and Vaccine 2, with bars of height 4, 5 and 9."
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "60%"
contrast_df |>
  mutate(Outcome = c(4, 5, 9)) |>
  ggplot(aes(`Predictor's categories`, Outcome)) +
  geom_col()
```

In this example:

- Contrast 1 compares Placebo with Vaccine 1
- Contrast 2 compares Placebo with Vaccine 2

However, I will not be able to compare Vaccine 1 and Vaccine 2. <!-- check: as on the slide, but with these codes the regression coefficients of the outcomes 4, 5 and 9 would be an intercept of 6 (the average of the three outcomes), -1 for Contrast 1 (5 minus 6) and 3 for Contrast 2 (9 minus 6), not the differences with Placebo (1 and 5) -->

```{r}
#| label: vaccine-models
#| include: false
vaccine_example <- tribble(
  ~category,   ~sum_contrast_1, ~sum_contrast_2, ~dummy_vaccine_1, ~dummy_vaccine_2, ~outcome,
  "Placebo",   -1,              -1,              0,                0,                4,
  "Vaccine 1",  1,               0,              1,                0,                5,
  "Vaccine 2",  0,               1,              0,                1,                9
)

vaccine_sum_zero <- coef(lm(outcome ~ sum_contrast_1 + sum_contrast_2, data = vaccine_example))
vaccine_dummy <- coef(lm(outcome ~ dummy_vaccine_1 + dummy_vaccine_2, data = vaccine_example))
```

::: {.callout-warning .box-mistake title="Common mistake: reading sum to zero contrasts as comparisons with the baseline"}
With the codes of @tbl-l05-sum-zero-example and the outcomes 4, 5 and 9, the regression gives an intercept of `r format_number(vaccine_sum_zero[[1]], 0)`, the average of the three outcomes. Contrast 1 gets `r format_number(vaccine_sum_zero[[2]], 0)` (5 minus 6) and Contrast 2 gets `r format_number(vaccine_sum_zero[[3]], 0)` (9 minus 6): each contrast compares one vaccine with the average of the three categories. To compare each vaccine with Placebo, use dummy codes with Placebo coded 0 in both: the estimates are then `r format_number(vaccine_dummy[[2]], 0)` and `r format_number(vaccine_dummy[[3]], 0)`.
:::

### Polynomial contrasts {#sec-l05-polynomial}

Polynomial contrasts are the most powerful of all the contrasts to test linear and non-linear effects: Contrast 1 is called Linear, Contrast 2 is Quadratic, Contrast 3 is Cubic, Contrast 4 is Quartic and so on. <!-- check: as on the slide, but nothing supports "the most powerful of all the contrasts", and the labels linear and quadratic only make sense for categories that are ordered, which is not the case of location (in the worked example below, poly_c2 compares Ireland with the two other locations) --> @tbl-l05-polynomial-example gives the codes of the three categories of a predictor (low, medium and high) and @fig-l05-polynomial-outcome the outcome of each category.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-polynomial-example
#| tbl-cap: "Polynomial contrasts for a predictor with three categories."
contrast_df <-
  tribble(
    ~`Predictor's categories`, ~Contrast_1, ~Contrast_2,
    "Low",                     -1,           1,
    "Medium",                   0,          -2,
    "High",                     1,           1
  )

contrast_df |>
  kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-polynomial-outcome
#| fig-cap: "Outcome of each category of the predictor."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of an outcome for the categories Low, Medium and High, with bars of height 4, 5 and 9."
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "60%"
contrast_df |>
  mutate(
    Outcome = c(4, 5, 9),
    `Predictor's categories` = factor(`Predictor's categories`, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(`Predictor's categories`, Outcome)) +
  geom_col()
```

In this example:

- Contrast 1 checks the linear increase between **Low**, **Medium** and **High**
- Contrast 2 checks the quadratic change between **Low**, **Medium** and **High**

If the hypothesis specified a linear increase, we would expect Contrast 1 to be significant but Contrast 2 to be non-significant.

```{r}
#| label: polynomial-model
#| include: false
polynomial_example <- tribble(
  ~category, ~contrast_1, ~contrast_2, ~outcome,
  "Low",     -1,           1,          4,
  "Medium",   0,          -2,          5,
  "High",     1,           1,          9
) |>
  mutate(category = factor(category, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")))

polynomial_estimates <- coef(lm(outcome ~ contrast_1 + contrast_2, data = polynomial_example))

polynomial_example <- polynomial_example |>
  mutate(linear_part = polynomial_estimates[[1]] + polynomial_estimates[[2]] * contrast_1)
```

@fig-l05-polynomial-parts shows what the two contrasts capture for the outcomes 4, 5 and 9. The estimates are an intercept of `r format_number(polynomial_estimates[[1]], 0)` (the average of the three outcomes), `r format_number(polynomial_estimates[[2]], 1)` for Contrast 1 and `r format_number(polynomial_estimates[[3]], 1)` for Contrast 2. Contrast 1 is the straight line from Low to High: its estimate is half of High minus Low, $(9 - 4) / 2$. Contrast 2 is what the straight line misses: Medium is below the line and the two ends are above it, a curve.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-polynomial-parts
#| fig-cap: "The outcomes 4, 5 and 9 (points) split into a linear part, the blue line of Contrast 1, and a quadratic part, the red distances of Contrast 2."
#| fig-alt: "Plot of the outcome for the categories Low, Medium and High, with points at 4, 5 and 9. A blue straight line goes through 3.5, 6 and 8.5 and is labelled Contrast 1 (linear), b = 2.5. Red segments join each point to the line: 0.5 above it for Low and High, 1 below it for Medium. They are labelled Contrast 2 (quadratic), b = 0.5."
#| fig-height: 3.4
ggplot(polynomial_example, aes(category, outcome)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = linear_part, group = 1), colour = book_col("blue"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = category, y = linear_part, yend = outcome), colour = book_col("red"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 1.3, y = 6.3, hjust = 0, size = 3.5, lineheight = 0.95,
    label = paste0("Contrast 1 (linear)\nb = ", format_number(polynomial_estimates[[2]], 1))
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 2.08, y = 5.5, hjust = 0, size = 3.5, lineheight = 0.95,
    label = paste0("Contrast 2 (quadratic)\nb = ", format_number(polynomial_estimates[[3]], 1))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(2, 10), breaks = seq(2, 10, 2)) +
  labs(x = "Predictor's categories", y = "Outcome")
```

### Worked example: comparing the results of different contrasts {#sec-l05-compare}

In the lecture, this example is demonstrated live. It shows what happens with different contrasts when comparing the average $js\_score$ according to the employee's $location$: **France**, **Ireland** and **Australia**. The contrast variables are first added to the data.

<!-- check: the slide code also creates treatment_c1 and treatment_c2, which are never shown or used -->

```{r}
#| label: contrast-variables
organisation_beta <- organisation_beta |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    treatment_c1 = case_when(
      location == "Ireland" ~ 1,
      location == "France" ~ 0,
      location == "Australia" ~ 0
    ),
    treatment_c2 = case_when(
      location == "Ireland" ~ 0,
      location == "France" ~ 0,
      location == "Australia" ~ 1
    ),
    sum_c1 = case_when(
      location == "Ireland" ~ 1,
      location == "France" ~ -1,
      location == "Australia" ~ 0
    ),
    sum_c2 = case_when(
      location == "Ireland" ~ 0,
      location == "France" ~ -1,
      location == "Australia" ~ 1
    ),
    poly_c1 = case_when(
      location == "Ireland" ~ 0,
      location == "France" ~ -1,
      location == "Australia" ~ 1
    ),
    poly_c2 = case_when(
      location == "Ireland" ~ -2,
      location == "France" ~ 1,
      location == "Australia" ~ 1
    )
  )
```

**Sum to zero contrasts.** @tbl-l05-sum-zero-codes gives the codes and @tbl-l05-sum-zero-lm the result of the linear regression of $js\_score$ on the two contrast variables.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-sum-zero-codes
#| tbl-cap: "Sum to zero contrast codes for the three locations."
tribble(
  ~category, ~sum_c1, ~sum_c2,
  "France",  -1,  -1,
  "Ireland",  1,   0,
  "Australia",    0,   1
) |>
  kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-sum-zero-lm
#| tbl-cap: "Linear regression of js_score on the two sum to zero contrasts."
lm(data = organisation_beta, formula = js_score ~ sum_c1 + sum_c2) |>
  tidy() |>
  mutate(p.value = format.pval(round(p.value, 3), eps = 0.001)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: sum-zero-model
#| include: false
model_sum_zero <- lm(js_score ~ sum_c1 + sum_c2, data = organisation_beta)
average_of_means <- mean(location_means$js_score)
```

@fig-l05-sum-zero-location shows what the two estimates measure. The intercept, `r format_number(coef(model_sum_zero)[[1]])`, is the average of the three group averages. The estimate of $sum\_c1$ is the distance from this value to the average of Ireland, and the estimate of $sum\_c2$ the distance to the average of Australia. France, coded -1 in both, is not compared with anything directly.

```{r}
#| label: fig-l05-sum-zero-location
#| fig-cap: "What the sum to zero contrasts of the worked example measure: the distance between the average of Ireland or of Australia and the average of the three group averages (dashed line)."
#| fig-alt: "Dot plot of job satisfaction for Australia, France and Ireland, with the employees as grey points and the average of each location as a blue point. A blue dashed line at 6.88 marks the average of the three group averages. A blue segment next to Ireland goes up from 6.88 to 8.16 and is labelled sum_c1, b = 1.28. A blue segment next to Australia goes down from 6.88 to 6.21 and is labelled sum_c2, b = -0.67."
#| fig-height: 3.8
sum_zero_distances <- location_means |>
  mutate(position = as.numeric(factor(location))) |>
  filter(location != "France") |>
  mutate(
    contrast = if_else(location == "Ireland", "sum_c1", "sum_c2"),
    estimate = js_score - average_of_means,
    label = paste0(contrast, "\nb = ", format_number(estimate))
  )

ggplot(organisation_beta, aes(location, js_score)) +
  geom_point(colour = book_col("grey"), size = 2.2, position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 1005)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = average_of_means, colour = book_col("blue"), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_segment(
    data = sum_zero_distances,
    aes(x = position + 0.22, xend = position + 0.22, y = average_of_means, yend = js_score),
    colour = book_col("blue"), linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  geom_point(data = location_means, colour = book_col("blue"), size = 3.5) +
  geom_text(
    data = sum_zero_distances,
    aes(x = position + 0.3, y = if_else(estimate > 0, (average_of_means + js_score) / 2, js_score - 0.45), label = label),
    hjust = 0, size = 3.4, lineheight = 0.95
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 3.3, y = average_of_means - 0.65, hjust = 0, size = 3.4, lineheight = 0.95,
    label = paste0("average of the three\ngroup averages = ", format_number(average_of_means))
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.5, 1.2))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(3, 10.5), breaks = seq(4, 10, 2)) +
  labs(x = "location", y = "js_score")
```

**Polynomial contrasts.** @tbl-l05-poly-codes gives the codes and @tbl-l05-poly-lm the result of the linear regression of $js\_score$ on the two contrast variables.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-poly-codes
#| tbl-cap: "Polynomial contrast codes for the three locations."
tribble(
  ~category, ~poly_c1, ~poly_c2,
  "France",  -1,   1,
  "Ireland",  0,  -2,
  "Australia",    1,   1
) |>
  kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-l05-poly-lm
#| tbl-cap: "Linear regression of js_score on the two polynomial contrasts."
lm(data = organisation_beta, formula = js_score ~ poly_c1 + poly_c2) |>
  tidy() |>
  mutate(p.value = format.pval(round(p.value, 3), eps = 0.001)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: polynomial-location-model
#| include: false
model_polynomial <- lm(js_score ~ poly_c1 + poly_c2, data = organisation_beta)
polynomial_location <- broom::tidy(model_polynomial)
```

::: {.callout-tip .box-example title="Example: reading the polynomial contrasts of location"}
The locations are not ordered, so read the codes as comparisons. $poly\_c1$ (France -1, Ireland 0, Australia 1) estimates half of Australia minus France: $b = `r format_number(polynomial_location$estimate[2])`$, $`r format_p(polynomial_location$p.value[2])`$. $poly\_c2$ (Ireland -2, France 1, Australia 1) compares Ireland with the two other locations: $b = `r format_number(polynomial_location$estimate[3])`$, $`r format_p(polynomial_location$p.value[3])`$. The estimate is negative because Ireland, coded -2, has the highest average: Irish employees are significantly more satisfied than the employees of France and Australia taken together.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .box-yourturn title="Your turn: create the sum to zero contrasts"}
1. Using the `organisation_beta.csv` file, create contrast variables to reproduce the results obtained with sum to zero contrasts.
2. When it is done, make explicit the hypotheses tested, the representation of the models and their corresponding equation.

Suggested time: 10 minutes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-solution title="Solution" collapse="true"}
**Variables**

- Outcome = $js\_score$ (from 0 to 10)
- Predictor 1 = $sum\_c1$ (Ireland vs. France)
- Predictor 2 = $sum\_c2$ (Australia vs. France)

**Hypotheses** <!-- check: with sum to zero codes, sum_c1 and sum_c2 test Ireland and Australia against the average of the three group means, not against France (here the sum_c1 estimate is 1.28, whereas the Ireland minus France difference is 1.90) -->

- $H_{a_1}$: The average $js\_score$ of Irish employees is different than the average $js\_score$ of French employees
    - $H_{0_1}$: The average $js\_score$ of Irish employees is the same as the average $js\_score$ of French employees
- $H_{a_2}$: The average $js\_score$ of Australian employees is different than the average $js\_score$ of French employees
    - $H_{0_2}$: The average $js\_score$ of Australian employees is the same as the average $js\_score$ of French employees

**Model.** @fig-l05-sum-zero-model represents the model, and its equation follows.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-l05-sum-zero-model
//| fig-cap: "The model with the two sum to zero contrasts as predictors of js_score."
//| fig-alt: "Diagram with two square boxes labelled sum_c1 and sum_c2, each with an arrow to a circle labelled js_score. The arrows are labelled b1 and b2."
//| fig-height: 2
//| fig-width: 5

digraph {
  graph [rankdir = LR]
  node [shape = circle]
  js_score
  node [shape = square]
  sum_c1, sum_c2

  sum_c1 -> js_score [label= b1]
  sum_c2 -> js_score [label= b2]
}
```

$$js\_score = b_{0} + b_{1}\,sum\_c1 + b_{2}\,sum\_c2 + e$$
:::

::: {.callout-note .box-keypoints title="Key points"}
- A categorical predictor with two categories is tested through the slope of the line between the two averages: if the averages are equal, the slope is 0. Reversing the codes of the two categories changes the sign of the estimate but not the $p$-value.
- With dummy coding (0 and 1), the category coded 0 becomes the intercept. With deviation coding (-1 and 1, or -0.5 and 0.5), the average of the categories becomes the intercept. The codes -0.5 and 0.5 keep a distance of 1 between the categories, which makes the estimate easier to interpret.
- The test of an interaction between two categorical predictors corresponds to the test of a variable resulting from the multiplication between their codes.
- In a predictor with three or more categories, each of the other categories is compared with a reference group (the first in alphabetical order). These comparisons do not give the overall effect of the predictor, which is tested with a one-way ANOVA (omnibus test).
- Post-hoc tests compare everything, which is why they can be considered as $p$-hacking. Contrasts test more precise hypotheses.
- The codes of a contrast follow three rules. Categories with the same code are tested together. The number of contrasts is the number of categories minus 1. The value 0 means the category is not taken into account, which is true when the model holds all the contrasts of the predictor and these contrasts are orthogonal, as the polynomial contrasts are.
:::

## Exercises {#sec-l05-exercises}

These exercises use the Organisation Beta data (`organisation_beta.csv`) and two small invented tables. Try each one before opening its solution. The first ones need only a pen, and the last ones need jamovi or R.

```{r}
#| label: exercise-models
#| include: false
# Invented averages for the exercises done by hand.
average_no_training <- 6.2
average_training <- 7.4

average_female_office <- 6.0
average_female_remote <- 7.0
average_male_office <- 6.5
average_male_remote <- 5.5

# Models of the data used in the exercises and in their solutions.
model_perf_c <- lm(js_score ~ perf_c, data = organisation_beta)
perf_c_anova <- anova(model_perf_c)
perf_c_means <- organisation_beta |>
  group_by(perf_c) |>
  summarise(n = n(), js_score = mean(js_score))
perf_c_mean <- function(level) {
  perf_c_means$js_score[perf_c_means$perf_c == level]
}

model_trend <- lm(js_score ~ C1 + C2, data = organisation_beta)
trend_estimates <- broom::tidy(model_trend)

model_salary_gender <- lm(js_score ~ salary * gender, data = organisation_beta)
salary_gender_estimates <- coef(model_salary_gender)
slope_female <- salary_gender_estimates[["salary"]]
slope_male <- salary_gender_estimates[["salary"]] + salary_gender_estimates[["salary:gendermale"]]

difference_ireland_france <- coef(model_location_france)[["locationIreland"]]
```

::: {#exr-l05-vocabulary}
## True or false?

Say whether each statement is true or false, and correct the false ones.

a. With dummy coding, the intercept is the average of the category coded 0.
